units.title: Count the additional call
units.rule: A call matches the current total wager. Subtract only what you already paid on this betting round. A payment on an earlier street does not pay a new bet.

example.prompt: Blinds are 1/2. You posted the big blind of 2 and face a raise to 8 total.
example.reason: Match 8 total after crediting the 2 already paid: 8 − 2 = 6 more. A raise to a total is different from adding that whole amount again.

cases.title: A blind already paid
cases.prompt: Blinds are 1/2. You posted the big blind of 2. The button raises to 9 total. You have enough counters to call; no one else changes the wager.
cases.question: How many additional counters does a call cost?
choices: 9 more.
Nine is the total you must reach. Your 2 on this round already pays part of it.
11 more.
Adding the posted blind to the total counts the forced post twice.
7 more.
Yes. The current total is 9 and you already paid 2 on this round: 9 − 2 = 7.
cases.reason: A call adds 7, bringing your contribution on this round to 9. This counts the price; it does not decide whether calling is good.

cases.title: A raise after your bet
cases.prompt: On the flop, you bet 5. Your one opponent raises to 17 total on this round. You have enough counters to call.
cases.question: How many additional counters would a call add?
choices: 17 more.
Seventeen is the opponent's total flop wager. Credit the 5 you already paid on the flop.
12 more.
Yes. Match 17 after subtracting your 5 on this same round.
22 more.
The raise is to 17 total, not by 17 on top of your bet of 5.
cases.reason: The additional call is 17 − 5 = 12. Preflop contributions do not enter this subtraction. Choosing an action requires more than counting its price.

cases.title: A new betting round
cases.prompt: You paid 12 on the flop. On the turn, you have paid nothing yet and your opponent bets 6. You have enough counters to call.
cases.question: How much does a turn call add now?
choices: 6 more.
Yes. You have paid zero on the turn, so the full new bet of 6 is owed.
Nothing; your earlier 12 covers it.
The flop payment stays in the pot. It is not a credit against a turn wager.
18 more.
The earlier 12 is already paid. It is not added to the new call amount.
cases.reason: Start the contribution count again on each street: 6 − 0 = 6 more on the turn. The pot still includes earlier payments.

units.title: Follow the action order
units.rule: At a six-player table, initial preflop action starts left of the big blind. After the flop, action starts with the first remaining player left of the button. A bet or raise can give a player another decision.

example.prompt: At a six-player table, the first three players fold. The button is deciding. Both blinds remain.
example.reason: After the button's initial action, the small blind and big blind still have initial decisions. Posting a forced blind did not use up their turns.

cases.title: Before the button
cases.prompt: Six seats in initial preflop order are: first seat, next seat, cutoff, button, small blind, big blind. The first two fold. You are the cutoff.
cases.question: After your initial action, which seats still have initial decisions?
choices: Only the small blind and big blind.
The button also remains after the cutoff in this initial order.
Button, small blind and big blind.
Yes. All three seats follow the cutoff in the initial preflop order.
Nobody; two folds end the round.
Folding removes those players from the hand. It does not remove the remaining players' decisions.
cases.reason: The button and both blinds still have initial decisions. This identifies the order without recommending a starting hand or an action.

cases.title: Two players remain
cases.prompt: This hand began with six players. After preflop action, only the button and big blind remain. The flop has just been dealt and nobody has acted on it.
cases.question: Who acts first on the flop?
choices: The big blind.
Yes. Among the remaining players, the big blind is first clockwise after the button.
The button.
The button is last in the initial postflop order here. Preflop and postflop starting points differ.
The player with the stronger cards.
Hand strength does not determine action order, and the private hands are not known to each other.
cases.reason: The big blind acts before the button on this flop. Two remaining players in a hand do not change the original button to someone else.

cases.title: A player gets another decision
cases.prompt: Only the big blind and button remain. On the flop, the big blind checks, the button bets 3, and the big blind raises to 9 total. Both have counters remaining.
cases.question: Whose decision is next?
choices: Nobody; the button already acted.
An earlier action does not settle a later unmatched raise.
The big blind again immediately.
The raise gives the other remaining player a decision before the raiser acts again.
The button, facing the raise.
Yes. The button must now respond to the big blind's unmatched raise.
cases.reason: The button has another decision. Calling, folding or making a legal raise can be available; checking does not match the new wager.

units.title: Separate a made hand and a draw
units.rule: Name the best hand you can make now. Then name a possible improvement separately. A flush needs five cards of one suit; four cards of that suit are not a completed flush.

example.prompt: You hold T♥ 9♥. The flop is T♠ 6♥ 2♥.
example.reason: The two tens make a pair. There are four hearts available, so you also have a heart-flush draw. Your pair exists now; the possible flush does not.

cases.title: Two features of one hand
cases.prompt: These are your two private cards and the three shared flop cards.
cases.question: Which description fits your cards now?
choices: A pair of queens and a heart-flush draw.
Yes. Your queen pairs the board's queen, and four hearts are available.
A completed heart flush.
There are four hearts, not the five needed for a flush.
A draw with no made pair.
The two queens already form a pair, even though the hand can also improve.
cases.reason: Your best five are Q-Q-J-8-3. The pair and the draw are separate facts. Neither establishes that you are ahead of an unknown opposing hand.

cases.title: A different flop
cases.prompt: Use your two private cards with this flop.
cases.question: What do you have now?
choices: A pair of aces.
Only one ace is available to you. A high private card is not a pair by itself.
A completed club flush.
Your two clubs plus two on the board make four clubs, not five.
Ace-high and a club-flush draw.
Yes. The five ranks are all different, and four clubs are available.
cases.reason: Your current made-hand category is high card. A possible club on a later street could improve it, but a draw is not a made flush or a guaranteed winner.

cases.title: A paired starting hand
cases.prompt: Use your two private cards with this flop.
cases.question: Which made hand can you build?
choices: Only a pair of eights.
Count the board's eight as well as your two private eights.
Three eights.
Yes. Your two eights and the board's eight make three of a kind.
A heart flush.
Only two hearts are available, both on the board. Five are required.
cases.reason: Three of a kind is available now. The king is a kicker, not a reason to discard the matching eight on the board.

units.title: Rebuild the best five on the river
units.rule: Choose the strongest five from your two private cards and the five shared cards. You may use zero, one or two private cards. Rebuild after each new card; your original hand label can become outdated.

example.prompt: You hold Q♠ T♠. The board ends Q♣ 6♠ 2♠ 8♦ 3♥.
example.reason: The flush missed: only four spades are available. Your best five are Q-Q-T-8-6, a pair of queens. Missing one improvement did not erase the pair.

cases.title: Two pairs on the board
cases.prompt: The river is dealt. Use these seven available cards.
cases.question: Which is your best five-card hand?
choices: Kings and queens are a stronger two-pair combination than kings and nines.
K-K-Q-Q-9.
Yes. Use the two higher board pairs and one nine as the kicker.
K-K-K-Q-Q.
Only two kings are available. You cannot create a third one.
cases.reason: Your pocket pair of nines is no longer one of the two pairs in your best five. One nine still supplies the kicker.

cases.title: A shared five-card hand
cases.prompt: The button holds the first private hand; the big blind shows the second. Compare both players on this completed board. There are no other players or side pots.
cases.question: Who has the better five-card hand?
choices: The button because it has a pocket pair.
A pair cannot improve on the board's ace-high straight.
The big blind because its private cards are higher.
Neither private hand improves on the same five-card straight available to both.
Neither. Both play the board and tie.
Yes. Both best hands are A-K-Q-J-T, with zero private cards used.
cases.reason: Both players have the same ace-high straight. Suits do not break this tie. Pot division and any odd counter follow the room's procedures; there is no sole winner of this showdown.

cases.title: One private card matters
cases.prompt: Choose from your two private cards and this completed board.
cases.question: Which five-card hand can you make?
choices: An ace-high heart flush: A♥ K♥ 8♥ 6♥ 3♥.
Yes. Your ace of hearts joins four hearts on the board; your jack does not play.
Only ace-high, because just one private card is a heart.
Hold'em permits using one private card. It does not require two private cards in the final five.
A jack-high straight.
These available ranks do not form five consecutive ranks.
cases.reason: Five hearts are now available. Count the cards you actually have, rather than carrying the earlier description of a draw into the river.

units.title: Separate facts and possible hands
units.rule: Known cards cannot also be in an opponent's hand. An action is an observation; the hidden cards and how often the opponent takes that action with each hand remain assumptions.

example.prompt: You hold A♠ Q♦ and the flop is J♥ 7♣ 2♦. Your opponent checks.
example.reason: The opponent cannot hold A♠ T♦ because you already have that exact ace. A check does not reveal the other cards or prove weakness. Other physically legal hands remain possible.

cases.title: Remove what is already known
cases.prompt: Your opponent checks. Consider only which exact private cards are physically possible, not how likely they are.
cases.question: Which opposing hand is still possible?
choices: K♠ A♣.
Your own king of spades cannot also be in the opponent's hand.
Q♥ Q♦.
The queen of hearts is already on the board.
Q♦ Q♣.
Yes. Neither exact card is in your hand or on the board. Possible does not mean likely.
cases.reason: Remove the five known cards before listing possible opposing holdings. A check does not eliminate the physically possible pair of queens.

cases.title: Read an observed action
cases.prompt: Your one opponent checks on this flop. No other information about that player is supplied.
cases.question: Which statement is an observed fact?
choices: The opponent checked; their hidden hand is not revealed.
Yes. That describes the action without turning an assumption into a fact.
The opponent has no ace.
A check does not show the hidden cards or rule out every legal ace.
Every possible hand is equally likely.
Physical possibility does not supply a frequency for each hand.
cases.reason: A range description separates known cards, legal possibilities and an assumption about frequencies. This scene supplies no measured frequency model.

cases.title: One revealed ending
cases.prompt: In one fictional river hand, an opponent bets, is called and reveals a bluff. No previous hands or population data are supplied.
cases.question: What does this single ending establish?
choices: The opponent always bluffs when betting the river.
One example is not a count of all the player's river bets.
This bet was a bluff; its frequency across other hands remains unknown.
Yes. One reveal establishes this ending, not a reliable frequency for future decisions.
Every earlier call against this player was correct.
This ending does not reconstruct the information or alternatives available in other decisions.
cases.reason: Record the observation separately from a frequency claim. Reviewing a decision still requires its earlier information and alternatives.

units.title: Name the purpose of a bet
units.rule: A value argument names worse hands that might call. A bluff argument names better hands that might fold. Compare a bet with checking when checking is available, and distinguish a supplied response pattern from evidence about real players.

example.prompt: A fictional river model says a worse pair will call your proposed bet. You are trying to get paid by that worse hand.
example.reason: That is a value argument. It identifies a response from a worse hand. It still does not establish a best bet size or prove betting is better than every alternative.

cases.title: A supplied response
cases.prompt: Nothing is owed on the river. In a hypothetical response model, some worse pairs call your proposed bet and no better hand folds. Your stated aim is to get called by those worse pairs.
cases.question: Which description matches that stated aim?
choices: Bluffing to make better hands fold.
The supplied model says no better hand folds. That is not the response named in your aim.
Seeking value from worse callers, while still needing to compare alternatives.
Yes. The proposed reason is getting paid by worse hands, not a proof of an optimal bet.
Proving a bet is best just because you hold a pair.
A hand label alone does not compare checking, sizing or the assumed responses.
cases.reason: The value argument names worse hands that pay. The scene supplies a hypothetical response, not an observed tendency of actual opponents.

cases.title: A different desired response
cases.prompt: On the river, your draw has missed. Nothing is owed. Your proposed bet is intended to make an opponent fold a better made hand. Whether they will do so often enough is not supplied.
cases.question: What is the stated purpose?
choices: A bluff intended to fold out a better hand.
Yes. The desired response is a fold from a hand that currently beats yours.
A value bet to get paid by worse hands.
The stated target is a better hand folding, not a worse hand calling.
A guaranteed profitable bet because a bluff is possible.
A possible fold does not establish its frequency or compare the bet with checking.
cases.reason: You can name the purpose without inventing a fold frequency. This does not establish that the bluff is good or supply a recommended action.

cases.title: Winning after a bet
cases.prompt: In one fictional hand, your river bet makes the opponent fold and you receive the pot. The opponent's hidden cards and response frequencies are not supplied.
cases.question: Which conclusion is supported by this ending?
choices: Every worse hand would have called.
The observed fold does not reveal all of the opponent's possible responses.
The bet was certainly better than checking.
One ending does not supply the comparison with checking or the full set of possible outcomes.
You won this pot; the ending alone does not grade the bet against checking.
Yes. The result is known. The value of the decision against alternatives still needs analysis.
cases.reason: Separate an observed result from the reason for an action. A useful review names what response was needed and what was known before the result.
